question_text: An ML engineer is building a fraud detection model. The training dataset contains 980000 legitimate transactions and only 2000 fraudulent transactions. If trained on this raw imbalanced data, the model is likely to classify everything as legitimate and achieve 99.8% accuracy while completely missing fraud cases. Which technique should the ML engineer apply to address this class imbalance?
explanation: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) is correct because it generates synthetic samples in the minority class by interpolating between existing minority examples, addressing the imbalance without exact duplication. Undersampling removes majority class rows and loses potentially useful data. One-hot encoding is a categorical feature encoding technique not a resampling technique. Normalization scales numeric feature ranges and has no effect on class distribution.
option_text: Apply undersampling to remove majority class rows until both classes are equal

question_text: A company is training an XGBoost model to predict insurance claim fraud. The training dataset has 97% legitimate claims and 3% fraudulent claims. The ML team wants to handle the class imbalance at the algorithm level without generating synthetic data or modifying the dataset. Which approach should the ML engineer take?
explanation: The scale_pos_weight hyperparameter in XGBoost directly handles class imbalance at the algorithm level by adjusting the weight of positive class examples in the loss function. Setting it to approximately 32 (97 divided by 3) tells XGBoost that misclassifying a fraud case should be penalized roughly 32 times more than misclassifying a legitimate case. SMOTE generates synthetic data which is a dataset-level approach not an algorithm-level one. Undersampling modifies the dataset. L2 regularization addresses overfitting not class imbalance.
option_text: Apply SMOTE to generate synthetic fraud samples before training

question_text: An ML team is splitting a credit default dataset for model training. The dataset is heavily imbalanced with 95% non-default and 5% default cases. The team randomly splits the data 80/20 for training and testing. After training, the model performs poorly at detecting defaults on the test set. What is the most likely data preparation mistake?
explanation: Random splitting on imbalanced data can accidentally concentrate most or all minority class (default) examples in either the training or test set. A stratified split preserves the class ratio in both training and test sets ensuring the model sees proportional examples of each class during training and is evaluated on a representative test set. Normalization affects feature scaling not class distribution. SMOTE should be applied after splitting not before. Increasing test size does not fix the underlying stratification problem.
option_text: The team should have normalized the features before splitting the dataset

question_text: A company operates an automated ML pipeline that ingests external vendor data daily for model retraining. SageMaker Model Monitor detects drift in deployed model inputs not ETL pipeline data quality. SageMaker Clarify measures demographic bias not uniqueness or completeness violations. Manual spot-checking is not scalable.
option_text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor on the training endpoint to detect data drift before each retraining run

question_text: An ML engineer reviews a data preparation pipeline for a hiring algorithm. SageMaker Clarify is run and reports: a Class Imbalance score of 0.45 for gender (75% male applicants), a DPL of 0.31 for gender (male applicants hired at significantly higher rates), and a Glue Data Quality rule violation where 8% of years_of_experience records contain negative values. The engineer must decide the correct order of remediation. Which sequence is correct?
explanation: The correct sequence is: first fix the Glue Data Quality violation (structural data integrity must be resolved before any analysis is meaningful — negative years of experience corrupts all downstream calculations), then address the DPL finding (label bias is the most severe fairness issue — it means historical hiring decisions encoded in the labels are themselves discriminatory), then address the Class Imbalance (representational imbalance is important but secondary to label bias since even a balanced dataset with biased labels produces a biased model).
option_text: Fix Class Imbalance first then DPL then data quality violations
